title: Storyboards and Shot Lists
objective: After this level you can explain how storyboards and shot lists plan a scene before a camera rolls.
summary: A storyboard draws a film shot by shot, a method the Disney studio pioneered; a shot list tracks every shot the crew must capture.

cards.headline: A film can be drawn, shot by shot, before a camera rolls.
cards.body: Filmmakers plan scenes on paper long before the shoot. Two documents do most of the work: a storyboard, which shows what each shot will look like, and a shot list, which keeps track of every shot the crew needs to film.

cards.headline: The storyboard: your film as a comic strip
cards.body: ACMI, a museum of screen culture in Melbourne, calls a storyboard a shot-by-shot visual plan that shows what a film will look like before it's shot. Each panel stands for one camera shot, and the board guides the team doing the filming. You don't draw every frame, and it needn't be art: stick figures will do, as long as the shot type and what's in it are clear.

cards.headline: A tool that grew up in animation
cards.body: The Walt Disney Family Museum says the Walt Disney Studios pioneered storyboarding. A storyboard maps out a story in a series of sketches, so filmmakers can see the plot in sequence and judge whether the story is clear. Laid out like that, plot holes and other inconsistencies are easier to spot.

cards.headline: The shot list: the checklist for the day
cards.body: A shot list keeps track of all your shots, ACMI explains, so when filming day comes you know exactly what you need to film. It can note each shot's camera movement, even when the answer is 'static', meaning the camera doesn't move. On set, filmmakers often keep the storyboard and script at hand too, to set up shots the way they planned.

cards.headline: Storyboards and shot lists: planned
learned: A storyboard: a shot-by-shot visual plan, one panel per shot
Stick figures are fine; clarity beats art
A shot list tracks every shot to film, even 'static' ones

questions.prompt: On a storyboard, each panel stands for one _____.

options.label: whole scene of the screenplay
options.rationale: A scene can need many shots; each panel is one shot.

options.label: day of the filming schedule
options.rationale: Schedules are planned elsewhere; panels show shots.

options.label: page of dialogue
options.rationale: Panels show what the camera sees, not pages of lines.

questions.explanation: A storyboard is a shot-by-shot plan: each panel represents one camera shot.

questions.prompt: Match each planning term with what it means.

pairs.right: Keeps track of all your shots

questions.explanation: A storyboard is a shot-by-shot visual plan, a shot list keeps track of all your shots, 'static' means the camera doesn't move, and the Walt Disney Studios pioneered storyboarding.

questions.prompt: A storyboard artist starts from the screenplay (Level 22). What does each scene heading tell them?

options.label: The camera angle for every shot
options.rationale: Scene headings give place and time, not camera angles.

options.label: Inside or outside, the place and the time of day
What each actor will wear
options.rationale: Costumes aren't part of the scene heading.

questions.explanation: A scene heading says INT. or EXT., names the place and gives the time of day.
